As of 300 PM EDT Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...An unsettled pattern prevails through midweek. Near 
average temperatures, humid conditions, and daily chances of showers 
and storms are expected.

Latest surface analysis depicted a cold front beginning to push into 
NW VA early this afternoon. Scattered showers and storms are 
beginning to develop along this front and are expected to gradually 
move SE into this evening with the slow FROPA. Models are in decent 
agreement with this line of showers and storms persisting through at 
least this evening and perhaps continuing into late tonight. HREF 
even maintains a 10% chance for 3"/3hr of rainfall across central VA 
through 11 PM. Will note that this area is in a locally lower PW 
(precipitable water) environment of 1.6-1.8" (as opposed to 
2.2-2.3" across extreme SE VA/NE NC) given some dry air 
entrainment with the cold front. This should limit the flash 
flooding risk today/tonight. However, with slow storm motions, 
the potential for risking PWs after sunset, and the potential 
for convection to linger around the Richmond Metro this evening 
(where flash flood guidance is only 1- 2"/1 hr and ~2"/3 hr, 
locally heavy rain and localized flash flooding remains 
possible. An additional area of scattered storms has developed 
across extreme SE VA/NE NC in association with an upper level 
trough centered across the Southeast. This convection is 
expected to move NE through the afternoon before tapering off 
this evening. Given the aforementioned locally higher PW 
environment in this region, locally heavy rainfall is possible. 
However, flash flood guidance is higher in this region (2.5-3"/1
hr) which leads to low confidence in reaching flash flooding 
criteria.

The cold front stalls near the VA/NC tonight/Tuesday morning 
before slowly lifting back north through the day Tuesday. 
Meanwhile, an upper level low becomes a cutoff low Tuesday 
across the southern Appalachians. This should help a weak 
surface low to form across the Carolinas Tuesday before lifting
north into central VA tonight. Given the W/E oriented front, 
surface winds should remain backed (predominantly E) through the
day on Tuesday with dew points remaining in the mid (locally 
upper) 70s. This should allow for enough instability (MLCAPE 
~1500 J/kg) for scattered to widespread showers and 
thunderstorms to develop Tuesday afternoon across 
southern/south- central VA and interior NE NC. PWs rise to 
2.2-2.5 across the area. These high PWs combined with 
tall/skinny CAPE, slow storm motion, and a nearly stationary 
front will likely lead to widespread showers and storms Tuesday 
afternoon into Tuesday evening. The aforementioned environment 
is favorable for locally heavy rainfall and isolated flash 
flooding. HREF probs for 3"/3hr increase to 30% generally south 
of I-64 during the afternoon. While normally this would be a 
borderline flood watch environment, the region of heaviest 
rainfall appears to be mainly south of Richmond and west of the
Hampton Roads region in an area of locally higher flash flood 
guidance (2.5-3"/1 hr and 3"+/3 hr). As such, the flash flooding
risk is more likely to be isolated in nature (as opposed to 
scattered). Convection tapers off from south to north Tue night.

Confidence is lower for widespread convection Wednesday 
afternoon. If widespread convection does occur on Tuesday, the 
environment may be too overturned to allow for much more than 
isolated to locally scattered showers and storms on Wednesday. 
However, given that Wednesday is still several days away and 
given that most CAMs do not go out that far, have kept NBM PoPs 
for Wed (for now). That being said, NBM PoPs appear high 
compared to what the general model consensus has been. If models
continue to not show much in the way of convection for Wednesday,
will likely need to lower PoPs.

Given the moist environment (and lack of DCAPE), relatively weak 
flow aloft, and tall/skinny CAPE, the main threat over the next few 
days will be locally heavy rain and flash flooding. As such, there 
is a marginal risk for excessive rainfall across most of the area 
today through Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Storm Prediction Center
(SPC) is not currently anticipating severe weather. 
Nevertheless, a few wet downbursts with mainly sub-severe storms
are possible. Otherwise, high temperatures dip down slightly 
below average Tuesday with near average temperatures expected 
on Wednesday.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A more typical summertime pattern returns for the 
latter half of the week. Isolated to scattered afternoon showers and 
thunderstorms remain possible, with near to slightly above normal 
temperatures prevailing through the weekend.
